cards.text: Meet the Teacher, who was king over Israel in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:12). This man already tried pleasure, building and gold, and found ALL of it futile (Ecclesiastes 2:1-11). Now he turns to consider wisdom and madness and folly, and asks what more the king's successor could do than what's already been done.

cards.question: The Teacher sets wisdom right next to folly and gives his verdict: wisdom exceeds folly, just as ___ exceeds darkness.

cards.text: The Teacher puts it this way: "The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness." Friend, I spent YEARS in the back of a junk drawer, so trust me, walking in darkness means apologizing to rubber bands you can't even see.

cards.question: Then the Teacher comes to realize something: the wise man and the fool each end up with a different fate.

cards.text: One fate for both, so the Teacher says to himself, "The fate of the fool will also befall me." He cracked open his own fortune cookie and did NOT like what it said.

cards.question: Wise or not, the Teacher is headed for the same fate as the fool. What does he ask himself next?

answers.text: What did being wise gain me
How can I grow even wiser

cards.question: The Teacher thinks about how people are remembered after they're gone. He says the wise man and the fool will both be ___ in the days to come.

cards.text: Then he says it straight: "Alas, the wise man will die just like the fool!" I think this one hits hard, friend.

cards.question: Wise or foolish, everyone dies and is forgotten. So what does the Teacher say about how he feels toward life?
The Teacher says he hated life. Why?

answers.text: The work people do was painful to him
The people he ruled turned from him
The enemies he faced took his city

cards.text: And the Teacher isn't done. He says he hated everything he had toiled for under the sun.

cards.question: The Teacher hated everything he had toiled for under the sun. Why?

answers.text: He must leave it to the man after him
It was all taken from him in battle
It had used up all his silver and gold

cards.text: Who knows whether that next man will be wise or foolish, the Teacher asks, yet he takes over ALL of it. Picture it, friend: I work all night on a perfect batch, crisp edges, every chip in place, and the next guy might use the box as a seat cushion.

cards.question: Thinking about all this, the Teacher's heart begins to find peace over all the labor he has done under the sun.
A man labors with wisdom, knowledge and skill, then must give his portion to a man who has not worked for it. The Teacher calls this futile and a great ___.

cards.text: Then the Teacher asks what a man really gets for all his toil and striving under the sun. All his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful.

cards.question: The man's days are full of grief. And even at night, the Teacher says, his ___ does not rest.

cards.text: No rest for that mind, even at night, and the Teacher calls this futile too. Your brain at three in the morning: "Hey. HEY. Remember that thing you said nine years ago?"

cards.question: Then the Teacher says nothing is better for a man than what?

answers.text: To eat and drink and enjoy his work
To gather more than anyone before him
To grow wiser than all his neighbors

cards.question: The Teacher says he has seen that eating, drinking and enjoying your work comes from the hand of God.

cards.text: Then he asks, "For apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?" Look at me, friend: years of no jokes in the dark, and it took the Most High reaching into a junk drawer before this stamper could enjoy his work again.
The Teacher says that to the man who is pleasing in His sight, God gives wisdom and knowledge and joy.

cards.question: The Teacher says God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the man who pleases Him. What task does the Teacher say God assigns to the sinner?

answers.text: Gathering what he'll hand to one who pleases God
Guarding the gates of Jerusalem through the night
Rebuilding the ruined walls of his own city

cards.text: And the Teacher closes it out: "This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind." Ever try to grab a breeze in your fist, friend? Open your hand. NOTHING.
